idiom_name: two hierarchies plus a delegated primitive interface (Abstraction holds an Implementor)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare an Implementor interface from primitive operations, give the Abstraction a reference to one, and implement every Abstraction operation in terms of those primitives; put variants of the high-level logic in refined abstractions that share the same reference. The choice of ConcreteImplementor belongs to the client, a factory or the DI wiring - never to the Abstraction itself. When the implementor is not meant to change during an object's lifetime, hold an immutable constructor-injected reference and document the invariants; when the implementor set is closed and you own all of it, consider exhaustive dispatch (sealed types, enums, variant types) instead of an open hierarchy. Additional guidance: treat the Implementor as a public SPI with its own artifact and semantic versioning; publish a compliance test suite that every new ConcreteImplementor must pass. When the implementor must notify the Abstraction, use a small separate listener interface rather than a concrete Abstraction reference. When the implementor set is closed and owned by your team, prefer sealed/exhaustive dispatch over an open virtual hierarchy to eliminate indirection cost. When an expensive implementor is stateless, share a single instance via Flyweight rather than allocating one per Abstraction instance.
pitfalls: Abstraction constructs a concrete implementor -> deployment selection and fake injection disappear -> inject the implementor through a constructor, factory or composition root.
Implementor methods mirror high-level policy -> every backend duplicates business decisions and drifts -> expose only stable primitives and keep orchestration in the Abstraction.

One stateful implementor is silently shared by unrelated abstractions -> buffers, connections or handles leak across clients -> share only stateless implementations or document ownership and lifecycle explicitly.
sources: Gamma et al. (1994), Bridge pattern, Design Patterns, p. 151.
